translations.text: Hymn of Judas Thomas, the apostle in the land of the Indians.
When I was a little child, living in my kingdom in my father’s house, I rested amid the [?] and splendors of those who raised me.
My parents equipped me and sent me from the East, our homeland. From the riches of our treasury they bound up a generous load for me.
It was large yet light, so that I could carry it alone: gold from Beth-Ellaye, silver from great Ganzak, and chalcedonies from India,
and agates from Beth-Kushan. They armed me with adamant, which crushes iron, and took off my splendid garment,
which they had made for me in their love, and my purple robe, woven and measured to fit my stature. They made an agreement with me
and wrote it in my heart so that it would not be forgotten: “If you go down into Egypt and bring back the one pearl that lies within the sea,
near the hissing serpent, you will put on your splendid garment and your robe that rests over it, and with your brother, our second in rank, you will be an heir in our kingdom.”
I left the East and went down, accompanied by two escorts, for the road was dangerous and difficult, and I was a child traveling it.
I crossed the borders of Mesene, the gathering place of the merchants of the East. I reached the land of Babylon and entered the walls of Sarbug.
I went down into Egypt, and my companions left me. I went straight toward the serpent and settled near its dwelling,
waiting for it to doze and fall asleep so that I could take my pearl from it. Since I was alone, I kept to myself; I was a stranger to those with whom I lodged.
There I saw someone of my own people, a freeborn man from the East—a handsome, devout young man, a son of anointing. He came and joined me.
I made him my trusted friend and took him as a partner in my trading. I warned him against the Egyptians and against associating with the unclean.
I dressed as they did, so that they would not recognize that I had come from outside to take the pearl, and would not rouse the serpent against me.
But somehow they realized that I was not their countryman. They dealt deceitfully with me and gave me their food to eat.
I forgot that I was a king’s son and served their king. I forgot the pearl for which my parents had sent me.
Weighed down by their food, I lay in a deep sleep. My parents learned of everything that had happened to me and grieved for me.
A proclamation went out in our kingdom that everyone should hasten to our gate: the kings and chiefs of Parthia and all the nobles of the East. They made a plan for me,
so that I would not be abandoned in Egypt. They wrote me a letter, and every noble put his name on it: “From your father, the King of Kings,
and your mother, ruler of the East, and from your brother, our second in rank, to you, our son in Egypt: greetings. Rouse yourself, rise from your sleep, and hear the words of our letter.
Remember that you are a king’s son. Look at whom you have served in slavery. Remember the pearl for which you were sent to Egypt.
Remember your splendid garment and recall your glorious robe, so that you may put them on and adorn yourself. Your name has been entered in the book of the valiant,
and with your brother [?] you will be in our kingdom.” My letter was a letter that the king had sealed with his right hand
against the wicked people of Babylon and the fierce demons of Sarbug. It flew and alighted beside me and became entirely speech.
At her voice and the sound of her movement, I stirred and rose from my sleep. I took her up and kissed her, and began to read her.
The words of my letter were written in accordance with what was inscribed on my heart. I remembered that I was a king’s son, and my noble birth asserted its nature.
I remembered the pearl for which I had been sent to Egypt. I began to enchant the terrible, hissing serpent. I lulled him and put him to sleep.
For I invoked my father’s name over him, and the name of our second in rank, and of my mother, the queen of the East. I snatched up the pearl and turned to go back to my father’s house.
I took off their filthy, unclean clothing and left it in their country. I directed my journey toward the light of our homeland, the East.
I found my letter, which had awakened me, ahead of me on the road. Just as she had awakened me with her voice, so now she shone her light upon me.
Clothed in silk, she shone before me with her appearance. With her voice and her guidance, she again encouraged me in my haste.
Her love drew me onward. I went out and passed through Sarbug. I left Babylon on my left and reached great Mesene, the merchants’ harbor,
which lies beside the sea. My parents sent there, from the heights of Rhamtha and Reken, my splendid robe, which I had taken off, and my toga, which was wrapped around it,
by the hands of their treasurers, who were entrusted with it because of their faithfulness. I had not remembered its appearance, for I had left it at my father’s house when I was a child.
Suddenly, when I encountered it, the garment became like a mirror to me. I saw all of it in my whole self, and I also encountered my whole self in it.
For we were two in distinction, yet again we were one in a single likeness. I also saw the treasurers who had brought it to me in the same way:
though they were two, they had one likeness, for the one seal of the king was marked upon them. Through their hands he restored to me my entrusted treasure and my wealth.
My splendid robe was adorned with glorious colors, with gold and beryls, rubies and agates, and sardonyxes of varied colors.
It had been prepared in its lofty home, and all its seams were fastened with diamonds. The whole image of the King of kings was depicted and portrayed all over it.
Its colors were also interwoven with sapphire. I saw, too, that movements of knowledge were stirring throughout it, and as though to speak,
I saw it preparing itself again. I heard the sound of its songs, which it uttered as it moved: “I belong to the one diligent in deeds,
for whom they raised me before my father.” I also perceived within myself that my stature was growing in keeping with his labors. With its royal movements,
it poured itself wholly toward me, and in the hands of those bringing it, it hastened for me to take it. Love also urged me
to run to meet it and receive it. I stretched out and received it. I adorned myself with the beauty of its colors, and my toga of brilliant colors
I wrapped entirely around myself. I put it on and ascended to the gate of greeting and homage. I bowed my head and worshiped the radiance of my father, who had sent it to me.
For I had carried out his commands, and he too had done what he promised. At the gate of his satraps, I mingled with his nobles.
He rejoiced in me and received me, and I was with him in his kingdom. With the sound of [?], all his servants praise him.
He promised that I would again be sent with him to the gate of the King of kings, and that with my offering and my pearl I would appear with him before our king.
The hymn of Judas Thomas the apostle, which he recited in prison, is finished.
